segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Pursue love, and be eager for the spiritual gifts, but even more that you may prophesy.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: For the one who speaks in a tongue speaks not to people but to God, for no one understands; rather, in the spirit he speaks secrets.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: But the one who prophesies speaks to people for building up and encouragement and comfort.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: The one who speaks in a tongue builds himself up, but the one who prophesies builds up the assembly.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: I want you all to speak in tongues, but even more that you may prophesy. The one who prophesies is greater than the one who speaks in tongues, unless he interprets, so that the assembly may receive building up.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: But now, brothers and sisters, if I come to you speaking in tongues, how will I benefit you unless I speak to you with a revelation or knowledge or prophecy or teaching?

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Even lifeless things that give a sound, whether pipe or lyre—if they make no distinction between the notes, how will anyone know what is being played on the pipe or the lyre?

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And if the trumpet gives an unclear sound, who will get ready for battle?

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: So it is with you: unless you give intelligible speech with your tongue, how will anyone know what is being said? You will be speaking into the air.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: There are who knows how many kinds of languages in the world, and none is without meaning.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: So if I do not know the meaning of the language, I will be a foreigner to the speaker, and the speaker a foreigner to me.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: So it is with you: since you are eager for manifestations of the Spirit, seek to abound in them for the building up of the assembly.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Therefore let the one who speaks in a tongue pray that he may interpret.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: For if I pray in a tongue, my spirit prays, but my mind is unfruitful.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: What then? I will pray with the spirit, but I will also pray with the mind; I will sing with the spirit, but I will also sing with the mind.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Otherwise, if you speak a blessing in the spirit, how will the one who fills the place of the uninstructed say “Amen” to your thanksgiving, since that person does not know what you are saying?

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: You, to be sure, are giving thanks well, but the other person is not being built up.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: I thank God that I speak in tongues more than all of you;

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: but in the assembly I would rather speak five words with my mind, so as to instruct others also, than ten thousand words in a tongue.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Brothers and sisters, do not be children in your thinking. In evil be infants, but in your thinking be mature.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: In the Law it is written:

segments.speaker: scripture
segments.text: “By people of other tongues and by the lips of others I will speak to this people, and not even so will they listen to me, says the Lord.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: So then, tongues serve as a sign not for those who believe but for unbelievers, while prophecy is not for unbelievers but for those who believe.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: So if the whole assembly comes together in one place and all speak in tongues, and uninstructed people or unbelievers come in, will they not say that you are out of your minds?

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: But if all prophesy, and some unbeliever or uninstructed person comes in, he is convicted by all, he is called to account by all,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: the hidden things of his heart are brought to light, and so, falling on his face, he will worship God, declaring,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “God is truly among you!”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: What then, brothers and sisters? When you come together, each one has a psalm, has a teaching, has a revelation, has a tongue, has an interpretation. Let everything be done for building up.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: If anyone speaks in a tongue, let it be two or at most three, each in turn, and let one person interpret.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: But if there is no interpreter, let the speaker be silent in the assembly and speak to himself and to God.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Let two or three prophets speak, and let the others weigh what is said.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: But if something is revealed to another who is sitting there, let the first be silent.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: For you can all prophesy one by one, so that all may learn and all be encouraged

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: (and the spirits of prophets are subject to prophets,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: for God is not a God of disorder but of peace), as in all the assemblies of the holy ones.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Let the women be silent in the assemblies, for they are not permitted to speak; rather, let them be subject, as the Law also says.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: If there is something they want to learn, let them ask their own husbands at home, for it is shameful for a woman to speak in the assembly.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Or did the word of God go out from you? Or has it reached only you?

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: If anyone thinks he is a prophet or a spiritual person, let him recognize that what I am writing to you is from the Lord.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: But if anyone does not recognize this, he is not recognized.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: So then, my brothers and sisters, be eager to prophesy, and do not forbid speaking in tongues;

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: but let everything be done decently and in order.

notes.note: In Jewish Greek of the period this is the ordinary word for a secret, especially something known to God and not disclosed. Modern “mystery” suggests a puzzle or something beyond understanding. Most English versions keep “mysteries” as an established term. Here the point is simply that what is said stays hidden from the hearers.

The Greek has no article and could mean the speaker’s own spirit or the Holy Spirit (“by the Spirit”). The lowercase reading is chosen because verse 14 speaks of “my spirit” praying in contrast with “my mind.” Many translations and commentators prefer “in the Spirit,” and Paul may not have drawn the line sharply.

A first-century hearer knew this word as a civic gathering and as the Greek Old Testament’s term for Israel assembled. “Church” is near-universal in English Bibles and readers know what it refers to, but it now suggests a building or an institution. In this chapter Paul has the actual gathered meeting in view.

The Greek plural was regularly used to address a mixed group of men and women, and Paul is addressing the whole community. Several modern versions also render it “brothers and sisters”; others keep “brothers” and explain the inclusive sense in a footnote.

The Greek says literally “eager for spirits.” Most interpreters take the plural as shorthand for the Spirit’s various workings, as in 12:7–11, and translations give “spiritual gifts” or “manifestations of the Spirit.” A minority think Paul is echoing the Corinthians’ own way of speaking about spirit-powers.

The Greek word means a layperson or non-expert as opposed to someone trained. Here it may be anyone in the meeting who cannot understand the tongue. Or it may be a distinct group, such as interested inquirers who are not yet believers, as verses 23–24 may suggest. Translations vary among “outsider,” “inquirer,” “ungifted” and “uninformed”; one neutral word is used in all three verses to leave the question open.

notes.phrase: In the Law it is written:
notes.note: The quotation is a free citation of Isaiah 28:11–12, where God warns Israel that, since they would not listen to plain speech, he will address them through the foreign language of invaders. Paul uses “the Law” broadly here for Scripture as a whole, not only the books of Moses. The same broad use may lie behind verse 34, where no specific passage is cited.

The word is used of all believers as people set apart for God, echoing the Greek Old Testament’s language for Israel. “Saints,” which many translations keep, now suggests canonized individuals or people of exceptional virtue. Other versions use “God’s people.”

notes.phrase: as in all the assemblies of the holy ones
notes.note: This phrase can be attached to what precedes, as here, following the punctuation of the SBLGNT, so that orderly prophecy is the practice of all the assemblies. Many translations instead begin a new sentence with it: “As in all the assemblies of the holy ones, let the women be silent.” The Greek allows either, and the choice affects how general the instruction in verse 34 sounds.

notes.phrase: Let the women be silent in the assemblies
notes.note: A few manuscripts, chiefly of the Western tradition, place verses 34–35 after verse 40. Partly for that reason, and because of the tension with 11:5 where women pray and prophesy, some scholars judge the two verses a later marginal comment that entered the text. Most editors and translations keep them here, since no surviving manuscript omits them. The SBLGNT prints them without brackets.

The Greek word means both “woman” and “wife,” and verse 35’s reference to “their own husbands” suggests married women are particularly in view. How far the silence extends is disputed. Since 11:5 assumes women pray and prophesy, many interpreters take it to restrict a particular kind of speaking, such as questioning or evaluating prophecies, and not all speech. Others read it as a general rule.

notes.traditional: is a command of the Lord
notes.note: Many manuscripts read “is a command of the Lord” or “are commands of the Lord,” and most English versions follow them. The SBLGNT adopts the shorter reading, without the word “command,” found in some witnesses. The sense is little affected.

Other manuscripts have an imperative, “let him be ignorant,” which the KJV follows. The reading translated here is a passive, which may mean not recognized by God or not recognized by the assembly as a prophet or spiritual person. The Greek plays on the verb “recognize” in verse 37.

candidates.reason: The plural address recurs throughout the letters and Acts, and versions split between “brothers” and “brothers and sisters,” so readers will notice inconsistency.
The same word means both “language” and the organ; whether “speaking in tongues” stays or becomes “languages” in Acts 2, 10, 19 and 1 Corinthians 12–14 needs one decision.
With its verb οἰκοδομέω it is a key Pauline metaphor, variously rendered “edification,” “upbuilding,” “strengthening” and “building up” across Romans, Corinthians and Ephesians.
It occurs in Acts 4:13, 2 Corinthians 11:6 and three times here, with renderings ranging from “outsider” to “untrained” to “ordinary,” and a consistent policy would help.
With παρακαλέω it ranges over “encouragement,” “comfort,” “exhortation” and “appeal” across the New Testament, and the choice of default affects many passages.
